items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: His wife Gladys, his first wife Gladys and I graduated from high school together, you know and we were all friends.

ctx.x: Well I’ve been in Carnegie Hall many a time and I’ve played there and felt very lucky to meet many great people, you know, Streisand and all them. But I’ve never felt like I felt that night cause we’d come, we’d come all the way, I’d seen it all the way. With John Levy you know. His wife Gladys, his first wife Gladys and I graduated from high school together, you know and we were all friends.

items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The main two that I – that were very important in my life – was Milt Hinton and Truck Parham. They were both excellent bass players, and they [were] patient and good teachers.

ctx.x: Then let’s back down the road. What was the early influence of music? Was it what? . . . in Chicago?

In grammar school there was no classes for music or anything. There was a singing class. I remember that. We’d sing little tunes, like you do – what do you call that?, where each one would take – one row would sing, “Row, row, row your boat.” That kind of stuff. Singing in the class. We would do those kind of things. But [there was] no actual teaching of music per se until you got to high school. When you got to high school, that’s when – like the schools that people like Nat Cole and Bill – William Hinton [sic:…
Before high school, in an academic sense, were there any teachers that stood out in your mind in terms of math or writing or any inspirations that you . . .?

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: I think they’re just real good friends. We’ve known each other for years... Milt Hinton had sort of, we were in school together and Milt had sort of helped me develop that instrument.

ctx.x: We are here today filming for the Hamilton Jazz Archive and we’re going to get a little different slant today. We’ve been talking to a lot of musicians about their experiences in the jazz world in association with Count Basie and Joe Williams. Today we have John Levy with us, who is a longtime friend, associate and manager with Joe Williams and we’re going to talk a little bit about how he looks at the music business. The business of music is something that sometimes musicians don’t deal with as much as they…

I think they’re just real good friends. We’ve known each other for years. In fact one of the first playing engagements of Milt Hinton, uh, Milt Jackson, was in Philadelphia. He and I and Tal Farlow worked in Philadelphia. That was one of the first playing gigs for Milt, you know, and so that’s how far back we go. We go back quite a way. And we were talking about that the other day, and I said, yeah, we go way, way back. And Joe I remember being a doorman at the Regal Theater and I used to go back stage and he…

items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had certain musicians help me, who were well schooled, like Milton Hinton... They helped me. They taught me.

ctx.x: Can you give us a sense of how you’re entering into the world of music, how that began to – those early years began to change your view of things? – how you began to see music as a way to make money, as a way to get that spot behind the desk?

It’s kind of hard for – your question. But anyway, music, it was just a means to an end. It was a means to make an extra amount of money to take care of a family once you got married. It was just a means. I wasn’t – there’s no special plan or no special idea about it. It was just – I could play a bass. I picked it up. I could play it. Then I had certain musicians help me, who were well schooled, like Milton Hinton and Truck Parham, who at that time – Milt ended up with Cab

Calloway and became a great, great player in the studios – great musician. They helped me. They taught me. In those days, musicians would help each other. If you heard something, they’d show you how to play it and how it worked, the fingering and all that sort of thing. I had books. I studied the books and practiced at home, but I didn’t really go in to have formal lessons. I was able to read, because having those lessons from the violin taught me time and all that, as far as notes were concerned. It was just in…
